title: Masculinity as Performance — The Cost of the Act
hook: Much of what passes for a man's natural body language is a performance learned in a schoolyard, kept up because the audience never seems to leave.
why:
Many of the habits this book has described as typical of men are not simply natural. The guarded face, the planted stance, the brief handshake, the slap that turns a hug into something tougher, the joke instead of the tears, the distance kept from a friend: these are learned, mostly in late childhood and adolescence, under the eyes of other boys. They are kept up because many men feel, rightly or wrongly, that they are always being watched and judged.

The performance has real benefits. It can earn respect, deter threats and make a man feel safe among other men. It also has costs, which research has begun to measure: anxiety when the act slips, aggression used to restore it, friendships that wither, feelings that go unexpressed and help that is never sought.

This chapter, the last before the book draws everything together, turns the lens on masculinity itself. It covers the idea that manhood must be earned and can be lost, how men prove it with their bodies, how boys learn the act, what it does to feelings and help-seeking, what researchers call the man box, how it shapes touch between men, and what changes when parts of the act are put down.

teach.p:
In 2008 Joseph Vandello, Jennifer Bosson and colleagues published five studies on what they called precarious manhood. Participants in the United States widely agreed that manhood, unlike womanhood, has to be earned and can be lost, and that it is proved through actions rather than given by biology. A man could stop being a real man by what he did; a woman was rarely thought to stop being a real woman in the same way.

The researchers then tested what happens when manhood is threatened. Men who were told that their answers on a test were typical of women, rather than men, afterwards completed more word fragments with words related to anxiety and, in a later study, with aggressive words. Women given the equivalent feedback showed no such effect. The threat to manhood was felt, and it was felt in a way that a threat to womanhood was not.

The authors noted that their participants were not representative of all cultures, and beliefs about manhood vary. But many men will recognise the underlying feeling: that being seen as a man is a test that never quite ends, and that a single lapse, a tear, a flinch, a soft word in the wrong company, can cost something.

The figure here stands with arms folded tightly and shoulders raised, gripping his own arm. It is the posture of a man on guard, and much of the time what he is guarding is not his body but his standing as a man.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if manhood were seen as a secure status, like womanhood. Vandello and colleagues found that people widely regard manhood as earned and losable, and that threats to it produce anxiety in men.
teach.pullQuote: Being seen as a man is a test that never quite ends.

teach.p:
If manhood can be lost, it can also be restored, and the body is one of the main ways men do it. In 2009 Bosson, Vandello and colleagues asked some men to braid hair on a mannequin, a task many associated with women, and others to braid rope. Afterwards, the men were offered a choice between punching a bag and solving a puzzle. Men who had braided hair more often chose to punch, and they punched harder.

In a further study, men who had their manhood threatened and were then allowed to display aggressive readiness showed fewer anxious thoughts afterwards. The display worked, in the sense that it made the men feel better. That is part of why such displays persist, even when they serve no other purpose.

Everyday versions are easy to see. A man who has been teased in front of his friends squares his shoulders, raises his voice or picks a fight. A man who has shown emotion makes a crude joke to cover it. A man who has lost an argument at work tightens his grip on the next handshake. Each is a small repair to a status that felt, for a moment, at risk.

The figure here raises his chin, throat exposed, the posture of a man presenting himself as unafraid. Sometimes it is pride; sometimes it is a repair. Knowing which may depend on what happened in the minutes before.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if threats to manhood had no effect on men's displays of aggression. Bosson and colleagues found that threatened men more often chose, and performed more forcefully, aggressive tasks.

teach.p:
In 2011 the developmental psychologist Niobe Way published Deep Secrets, based on years of interviews with boys in the United States as they moved from early to late adolescence. In early adolescence, many boys spoke about their closest friends with startling tenderness. They described loving them, needing them, sharing secrets with them, and feeling lost without them.

By late adolescence, many of the same boys described losing those friendships. They talked of not trusting other boys, of keeping things to themselves, and of distancing themselves from closeness that might be read as gay. The language of love was replaced by the language of autonomy and toughness, and many said that they missed what they had lost.

The body records the change. Boys who once leaned on each other, slept over and walked arm in arm learn to stand apart, to greet with a nod or a punch on the arm, to keep a careful space on a sofa, to turn affection into mockery. Part III's chapters on friendship between men described how these habits persist into adulthood, and how much they cost men in later life.

The figures here stand side by side, a careful gap between them. Many men stand this way with their closest friends, without remembering that they once did not.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if boys' friendships stayed equally close and expressive through adolescence. Way's interviews found that many boys moved from open intimacy to guardedness and lost the friendships they had valued most.

teach.p:
Among the earliest lessons many boys learn is which feelings may be shown. Anger is often allowed; fear, sadness, hurt and tenderness often are not. Over time, many men become skilled at keeping these off their faces: the jaw set, the eyes turned away, the swallow, the change of subject, the joke. Part II described how much of this is held in the body, in tension and in breath.

In 2017 Joel Wong and colleagues combined seventy-eight samples, with nearly twenty thousand participants, that measured how strongly men conformed to traditional masculine norms. Conformity was modestly linked to poorer mental health and more strongly to less willingness to seek psychological help. Not every norm mattered equally: self-reliance, along with norms about sexual conquest and power over women, was among the most consistently linked to poor outcomes.

The practical consequence is that men in distress often look fine. They keep working, keep joking, keep their faces composed, and seek help late or not at all. A man's irritability, drinking, withdrawal or sudden anger may be the only visible form of grief, fear or depression he allows himself.

The figure here looks away, his face turned from the person in front of him. It can be a man thinking, or a man keeping something from showing. Earlier chapters said it plainly: the face is not a reliable window, and in men taught to guard it, it may be a closed one.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if conformity to masculine norms had no link with men's mental health or help-seeking. Wong and colleagues found that conformity, especially to self-reliance, was linked to poorer mental health and less help-seeking.
teach.pullQuote: A man's anger may be the only visible form of grief or fear he allows himself.

teach.p:
In 2017 the organisation Promundo, now called Equimundo, surveyed about 3,600 men aged eighteen to thirty in the United States, the United Kingdom and Mexico. It used the image of a man box: a set of rules about being self-sufficient, acting tough, being physically attractive, sticking to rigid gender roles, being heterosexual, being sexually dominant and using aggression to resolve conflict.

Young men who agreed most strongly with these rules, those inside the box, were about twice as likely as those outside it to report having had suicidal thoughts in the previous two weeks, with the difference largest in the United Kingdom. They were more likely to have bullied others or been bullied, and at least three times as likely to report having made unwanted sexual comments to women.

The survey also found a gap. Far more young men said that society sent them these messages than said they personally agreed with them. The audience is real, and the pressure it applies is real. But the gap suggests that part of the performance is put on for an audience that is less demanding, man by man, than it seems as a whole.

The figures here stand in a loose circle, three men facing each other. Much of the policing of masculinity happens in groups like this one, often through jokes, and often by men who privately agree with the person being policed.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if strong adherence to these rules had no link with young men's well-being or behaviour. The Man Box survey found that men inside the box reported more suicidal thoughts, more bullying and more harassment of women.

teach.p:
The performance of masculinity shows nowhere more clearly than in how men touch each other. Part III described the coded forms that touch between men often takes in English-speaking countries: the handshake pulled into a half hug, closed with two hard slaps on the back; the punch on the arm; the headlock; the arm around the shoulder that turns into a shove. Each allows contact while signalling that it means nothing soft.

These codes are not universal. In many parts of South Asia, the Middle East and Africa, men friends hold hands, walk arm in arm and sit close without any suggestion of romance, as an earlier chapter in this part described. Older European and American photographs show men posing with arms around each other and heads together in ways that would draw jokes today. The rules are cultural and recent, not natural.

For many men, the result is a kind of touch hunger. Men who rarely touch anyone outside a romantic partner may feel the absence acutely after a divorce, a bereavement or a move, and may not have words for it.

The figures here greet in the classic way: a grip pulled into a brief half embrace. It is warm, and it is also carefully limited. Noticing the limits is not the same as abandoning them; it is the first step in deciding which ones you still want.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if the forms of touch allowed between men were the same in all times and places. Accounts from many cultures and from earlier generations show much freer touch between male friends.

teach.p:
Not all of the performance is a burden. Steadiness under pressure, physical courage, protectiveness and restraint are valued by many men and by the people who rely on them. The aim is not to abandon them but to choose: to keep the parts of the act that serve you and the people you love, and to put down the parts that cost more than they give.

Men who have put down parts of the act often describe small, specific changes. Telling a close friend the truth when asked how they are. Letting a hug last a second longer. Crying at a funeral without apologising. Asking for help with a problem before it becomes a crisis. Holding a son's hand past the age when other fathers stop. Sitting with a friend in trouble without needing to fix anything.

For readers of other men, the chapter suggests a few things. A man's composure may be hiding more than it shows. His anger may stand in for fear or grief. Side-by-side settings, a walk, a drive, a shared task, may let him say what a face-to-face conversation would not. And men in groups often hold back from kindness because they think the others would mock it, when many of the others are waiting for someone to go first.

The figures here show one of the simplest gestures between men: a hand on the shoulder of a friend whose head is bowed. It asks for nothing, it can be shrugged off, and for many men it is the first step out of the box.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if men's distress were always visible, or if group norms about masculinity were as strongly held as men assume. The Man Box survey found that far more young men felt society pressed these rules on them than personally agreed with them.

poseGallery.doCaption: Letting it down where it is safe
poseGallery.dontCaption: Keeping the guard up even with friends
poseGallery.annotation: The guard has its uses. Notice the places where you no longer need it, and let it drop there.

poseGallery.dontCaption: Looking away from a friend's distress
poseGallery.annotation: You do not need the right words. A hand on the shoulder and your presence say more than a change of subject.

poseGallery.doCaption: Letting the hug mean what it means
poseGallery.dontCaption: Keeping a close friend at arm's length
poseGallery.annotation: With a close friend, a hug held a moment longer, without the back slaps, is not a loss of anything.

caseStudy:
Callum, twenty-nine, has had the same four close friends since school. They see each other most weekends, mostly at the pub or watching football, and their conversation runs on banter: who is losing his hair, who cannot cook, whose team is the worst. Callum loves them, though none of them has ever said anything of the kind to each other.

When Ben's father died suddenly, the group did what it always did. They took him to the pub, bought his drinks and kept the jokes going. Ben laughed along and said he was fine. Over the next two months he stopped coming out, answered messages with a thumbs-up, and once snapped at Callum over nothing.

Callum talked to his partner, who asked whether any of them had actually asked Ben how he was, alone, without the others. None had. Callum felt the old reluctance: it would be awkward, Ben would think he had gone soft, the others would hear about it.

He went round anyway, with the excuse of returning a drill. They ended up fixing a shelf together in Ben's hallway, and halfway through, without looking up, Callum said that he was sorry about Ben's dad and that he had not known what to say. Ben stopped, sat on the stairs, and cried for the first time since the funeral. Callum sat next to him with a hand on his shoulder and said nothing at all.

Later, Ben told him that he had been waiting for one of them to ask. The group still runs on banter. But Callum now sends Ben a message every few weeks that is not a joke, and the others, it turns out, have started doing the same.
observe: Notice, in a group of men, how emotions other than anger are handled: by jokes, by changing the subject, or by silence.
Notice the forms of touch between men around you, and how often a warm gesture is closed with a slap, a shove or a joke.
Notice any moment this week when you held back a feeling, a word or a gesture because of how other men might see it.
Notice which men in your life you can be honest with, and what makes them different.

drills.name: The Audience Check
steps: Think of a feeling or gesture you regularly hold back in front of other men.
Write down who you imagine would judge it, and what they would think.
Ask whether you have evidence that they would, or whether you are assuming it.
Choose one person with whom you could test the assumption.

drills.name: One True Answer
steps: The next time a close friend asks how you are, notice the reflex answer forming.
Pause, and give a true answer instead, even a short one.
Write a sentence about what happened.

drills.name: Side by Side
steps: Think of a man in your life who may be struggling and not saying so.
Invite him to something you can do side by side: a walk, a drive, a job, a match.
During it, ask one real question, and then let the silence do some work.
Do not try to fix anything unless he asks.

drills.name: Keep and Put Down
steps: List the parts of the masculine performance you learned growing up: in face, voice, posture, touch and words.
Mark the ones that still serve you and the people you love.
Mark the ones that cost more than they give.
Choose one to practise putting down this month, and one to keep with pride.

quiz.q: A friend says that real men do not need to talk about their feelings, and that those who do are weak. What does this chapter suggest?
options: He is right, since keeping feelings to yourself is what protects men's mental health over time
Self-reliance norms are linked to poorer mental health and less help-seeking, not to strength
He is right for some feelings, since only fear and sadness ever need to be hidden from others
Men should share every feeling with everyone they meet, since any restraint at all is harmful
quiz.explain: Wong and colleagues found that conformity to masculine norms, especially self-reliance, was linked to poorer mental health and much less help-seeking. Keeping feelings hidden is not the same as being strong.

quiz.q: What did Vandello and colleagues find in their 2008 studies of precarious manhood?
options: Manhood was seen as a status to be earned and kept, and threats to it made men anxious
Manhood and womanhood were both seen as secure states, given at birth and never lost
Womanhood was seen as more precarious than manhood, and harder to earn and to keep
Threats to gender made both men and women equally anxious, in exactly the same way
quiz.explain: Participants saw manhood, unlike womanhood, as earned and losable. Men whose manhood was threatened showed more anxiety-related thoughts, while women given similar feedback did not.

quiz.q: In Bosson and colleagues' 2009 experiments, what did men who had braided hair go on to do?
options: They avoided all physical tasks and chose to solve a quiet puzzle on their own instead
They behaved no differently from the men who had braided rope rather than hair
They more often chose to punch a bag rather than do a puzzle, and punched it harder
They asked to braid more hair, having found that they enjoyed the task more than expected
quiz.explain: Men whose manhood had been threatened more often chose the aggressive task and performed it more forcefully. A display of aggression helped restore a status that felt at risk.

quiz.q: What did Niobe Way find in her interviews with boys over the course of adolescence?
options: Boys' friendships grew steadily closer and more open as they moved into late adolescence
Boys had no close friendships at any age, and showed no interest in having any at all
Boys spoke of friendship only in terms of sport and competition, at every age studied
Younger boys spoke openly of loving friends, but many lost those friendships later on
quiz.explain: In early adolescence many boys described deep, tender friendships. By late adolescence many had become guarded, distanced themselves from closeness, and missed what they had lost.

quiz.q: A friend whose father has just died keeps making jokes and insists he is fine, but has stopped coming out. What fits this chapter best?
options: Take him at his word, since pressing a man about his feelings will only embarrass him
Find a side-by-side activity with him alone, ask once, and be ready to just sit with it
Tell the rest of the group that he is struggling, so that they all go easier on him
Insist that he sees a counsellor straight away, and keep raising it until he agrees
quiz.explain: His jokes and withdrawal may be the only forms his grief is allowed to take. A side-by-side setting, one real question and quiet company often open more than direct pressure.

quiz.q: Your teenage son and his best friend used to hug and sprawl on the sofa together, but now keep a careful distance and joke about not being gay. What fits this chapter best?
options: Encourage the distance, since it shows that he is growing up into a normal young man
Tease him about it, so that he sees how silly the jokes are and gives them up
Recognise the pressure behind it, and make home a place where closeness is not mocked
Ban the friend from the house, since the jokes are clearly a sign of a bad influence
quiz.explain: Way's research describes exactly this shift, driven by fear of how closeness will be read. A home where affection between boys is never mocked gives it somewhere to survive.

reflection.prompt: Think of one specific part of the masculine performance that you learned as a boy: a way of standing, greeting, touching, joking or keeping your face still. Describe where and from whom you learned it, and who the audience was. Then describe a recent moment when you used it. Did it serve you, or did it cost you something? What would it look like to keep it where it helps, and put it down where it does not?
reflection.guidance: This is personal territory, and the performance may feel like simply who you are. Write about specific behaviours and specific moments rather than about masculinity in general. There is no need to reject everything you learned; the aim is to see it clearly enough to choose.

failureMode: The first failure is to mistake the performance for nature, and to treat men who step outside it as weak or strange. The second is to read a man's composure as proof that he is fine, when men taught to guard their faces often look fine until they are not. The third is to miss anger, drinking or withdrawal as the forms that grief, fear and depression take in many men. The fourth is to police other men, through jokes and mockery, for closeness or feeling. The fifth is to assume that other men hold the rules more strongly than they do, and so never be the first to break them. And the sixth is to throw away the whole of the performance, including the parts that genuinely serve you and others.

watch.title: The Mask You Live In: Official Trailer
watch.notice: A documentary about how boys in the United States learn to be men. Notice the phrases the boys have been told, and how they describe keeping their feelings off their faces.

watch.title: Close: Official Preview
watch.notice: A film about two thirteen-year-old boys whose easy, physical friendship comes under pressure when classmates start asking what they are to each other. Watch how freely the boys move together, and compare it with how men you know stand with their friends.

watch.title: Moonlight: Decide for Yourself
watch.notice: An older man talks to a boy about deciding who he is going to be, rather than letting others decide it for him. Notice the tenderness in how the man holds himself with the boy.

reviewPrompt: This week, give one true answer when a friend asks how you are, and let one hug last a moment longer.
